title: After Scripture's light: how it is perceived; fleeting opinion versus true saving faith without the Spirit's inward work
pass_a_gloss: In the previous disputation we set out what light Scripture has — that is, what arguments and marks of truth and of divine origin. It follows that we should ask how that light is perceived, and whether, and how far, the Holy Spirit's work is necessary for us to acknowledge Scripture as true and divine. Here, however, one must distinguish between a certain fleeting and vanishing opinion and true saving faith, which is pleasing and acceptable to God. For someone can form a certain opinion of Scripture's divinity, led to it by some human incentives, without any inward operation of the Spirit: and this is what the Schools call human and acquired faith. So many most wicked and most perverse heretics do not deny Scripture's authority and acknowledge it as divinely inspired. Indeed the unbelieving Jews themselves fiercely defend at least the Old Testament's authority; and the Mohammedans are said to hold and revere the books of both Testaments as divine. Yet it is not necessary that we suppose the Holy Spirit to be at work in all those heretics and unbelievers, illuminating their minds within.
pass_b_english: In the previous disputation we set out what light sacred Scripture has — that is, what arguments and marks of truth and of divine origin. Next we ask how that light is perceived, and whether, and how far, the Holy Spirit's work is needed if we are to acknowledge Scripture as true and divine.

Here, though, we must distinguish a fleeting, vanishing opinion from true saving faith that is pleasing and acceptable to God. A person can form an opinion that Scripture is divine, drawn by some human incentives, without any inward work of the Spirit; the Schools call that human and acquired faith. Many utterly wicked and perverse heretics do not deny Scripture's authority and grant that it is divinely inspired. Unbelieving Jews themselves fiercely defend at least the Old Testament's authority, and Mohammedans are said to hold and revere both Testaments as divine. Still we need not suppose that the Holy Spirit is at work in all those heretics and unbelievers, illuminating their minds within.
source_text:
I. Superiori disputatione exposuimus quam lucem, id est, quae argumenta et indicia Veritatis, et originis divinae, habeat Scriptura sacra: sequitur ut inquiramus, quomodo lux illa percipitur, Et An, et Quousque opera Spiritus sancti necessaria sit, ut Scripturam pro vera et divina agnoscamus.

II. Hic autem distinguendum est, inter opinionem quandam fluxam et evanidam, et fidem veram et salutarem, quae Deo sit grata et accepta. Quandam enim opinionem de Scripturae divinitate potest aliquis concipere, eo adductus humanis quibusdam incitamentis, absque ulla Spiritus interna operatione: atque haec est quam Scholae fidem humanam et acquisitam vocant. Sic haeretici multi improbissimi et perversissimi authoritatem Scripturae non negant, illamque divinitus inspiratam agnoscunt. Imo Judaei ipsi infideles Veteris saltem Testamenti authoritatem acriter defendunt: Mahumetani vero utriusque Testamenti libros pro divinis habere, et revereri, perhibentur. Neque tamen necesse est, ut in omnibus illis haereticis et infidelibus Spiritum sanctum agere putemus, et intus eorum mentes illuminare.
